episode_thesis: Alan Dunne argues that debt, deficits and policy trends over three decades point to structurally higher US bond yields ('all roads lead to higher yields'): bond-market discipline of fiscal policy has weakened, rates above growth make debt dynamics self-reinforcing, and most scenarios end in financial repression or fiscal dominance. For asset allocation he recommends scenario-based construction instead of anchoring on 1980-2020, and notes that forward-looking return estimates point to below-average equity returns. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen reviews a weak May 2025 for trend followers (medium-term models hit hardest) and argues that, because scenario selection can go wrong and unforeseen risks cannot be listed, a regime-agnostic, non-predictive trend allocation is useful and should not be timed on macro or political views; Alan agrees.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.role: Co-host; allocator/researcher; writes the Substack 'Beyond the Cycle'; Dublin-based
speakers.speaker_note: Ledger spelling 'Alan Dunne' kept (captions give 'Alan Don'). Corrections applied: MT072-C17-3 (linking trend allocation to a macro view works for a year, then something surprises) and MT072-C17-6 (the 2016-2022 timing example ending 'Don't try and time it') are Alan's, not Niels's. worldview_premises.premise: Bond-market discipline of US fiscal policy has weakened: in 1993 a deficit of about 4% of GDP and debt of 45% of GDP intimidated politicians, whereas today debt is about 100% of GDP (net of agency holdings) and the 2025 budget bill adds nearly 4 trillion over ten years.
worldview_premises.support: 1993 Carville quote and numbers from memory; current debt/deficit figures.

worldview_premises.premise: In the 1990s, deficit reduction (Clinton tax hikes) let the Fed ease and lowered yields, fuelling investment; the opposite fiscal stance today does not help.
worldview_premises.support: Greenspan-Clinton conversation as recounted; a 1990s productivity boom helped as well.

worldview_premises.premise: From 2017 the US ran large deficits at full employment (a procyclical turning point), followed by MMT ideas and huge Covid spending; the end of the neoliberal era removed ideological appetite for cutting deficits.
worldview_premises.support: Chronology of US fiscal policy 2017-2025; guest Gary Gerstle cited.

worldview_premises.premise: High public debt levels are here to stay (Eichengreen); the 2021-22 inflation eroded real debt, but disinflation reverses this, so the debt burden rises again.
worldview_premises.support: Jackson Hole paper by Barry Eichengreen and a conversation with him.

worldview_premises.premise: When interest rates exceed growth (R greater than G) debt service takes a growing share of resources and debt becomes unsustainable regardless of the debt/GDP level.
worldview_premises.support: Standard debt-dynamics arithmetic.

worldview_premises.premise: Higher yields make debt less sustainable, which raises yields further: a self-reinforcing loop.
worldview_premises.support: Argument from fiscal arithmetic.

worldview_premises.premise: Fiscal crises develop slowly then move fast (Dornbusch), so the timing of the bond break is hard to call while the direction is clear.
worldview_premises.support: Rudi Dornbusch quote.

worldview_premises.premise: Most scenarios end in financial repression or fiscal dominance (forced bond buying or easier-than-warranted policy); politicians act on deficits only after a crisis forces them to.
worldview_premises.support: Political-economy reasoning, no precedent beyond the 1990s contrast.

worldview_premises.premise: Growth is unlikely to fix the debt soon: labour force limits (immigration, ageing) and a 10-15 year lag from new technology (AI) to productivity gains.
worldview_premises.support: Internet and computers lag as precedent; contrast with post-WWII growth.

worldview_premises.premise: A negative stock-bond correlation let investors accept a low term premium; as that hedge value fades they require a higher yield, so real yields can decouple from inflation.
worldview_premises.support: Portfolio-role argument; real yields about 2% now, over 3% in 1993.

worldview_premises.premise: Reindustrialising a full-employment US economy creates bottlenecks, skill shortages and wage pressure that may spill over into broad inflation, though the tariff effect cannot be modelled with conviction.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from labour market slack.

worldview_premises.premise: Private equity and private credit are less diversifying than assumed: low distributions (DPI) constrain new flows, the last buyer may be retail, and private credit holds the same sectors and weaker ratings.
worldview_premises.support: Conversations with institutional investors and listened-to discussions.

worldview_premises.premise: The BOJ's bond purchases moved losses from the private sector to the central bank, so the JGB yield rise did not cause private-sector stress or a yen carry unwind.
worldview_premises.support: Observation that dollar-yen stayed in range; insurers possibly shifting from 40-year to 10-year bonds.

worldview_premises.premise: Asset allocation inputs should not be anchored on one period such as 1980-2020, which was favoured by disinflation and falling yields; use scenario-based construction and robustness to volatility and correlation assumptions.
worldview_premises.support: Investor questions and the shift from the 1980-2020 regime.

worldview_premises.premise: Forward-looking return estimates (dividend yield plus earnings growth) correlate positively with realised 10-year returns, whereas trailing past returns correlate negatively; realised returns overshoot high estimates and undershoot low ones.
worldview_premises.support: AQR papers and examples (2010 estimate 8-10% vs 15% realised; 2000 estimate 3-4% vs flat).

worldview_premises.premise: US outperformance came largely from re-rating (CAPE from about half of non-US in 1990 to double today), so mean reversion argues for less US bullishness; if the US is safer its required return is lower (Dimson).
worldview_premises.support: AQR paper and a conversation with Elroy Dimson.

worldview_premises.premise: Large equity drawdowns follow periods of optimism and rich valuations, as in 2000, not pessimism.
worldview_premises.support: Dimson's point; 2000 as example.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend allocations should not be linked to a macro view or political backdrop; waiting for conditions to look favourable misses years.
worldview_premises.support: 2016-2022 example: a 'central banks control markets' view held for a year or two, 2019-2021 were good for trend, consensus only in 2022.

worldview_premises.premise: True diversification means balancing across risk factors; equities, private equity and credit share the same tail risk.
worldview_premises.support: Argument that these assets share a big negative tail.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why all roads lead to higher US yields

steps.from: Large deficits at full employment, no ideological appetite for restraint, 2025 budget bill adding nearly 4 trillion
steps.why: Procyclical fiscal stance since 2017, end of the neoliberal era, disinflation reversing the 2021-22 erosion of real debt.

steps.from: Rising debt with weak bond-market discipline and Treasury leaning on bills
steps.to: Doubts about demand at the long end and a higher term premium
steps.why: Less hedge value from bonds and more supply require a higher yield.

steps.from: Yields of 5% or more versus nominal GDP growth of 4-4.5%
steps.to: R above G, worse fiscal arithmetic, and a vicious cycle of higher yields
steps.why: Debt service takes a growing share of resources.

steps.to: Financial repression or fiscal dominance as the likely end state
steps.why: Forced buying by the Fed or private sector, or easier-than-warranted policy, e.g. a Fed chair under administration influence after Powell's term ends in 2026 (Nixon-Burns).

steps.to: Stops only with a credible deficit policy
steps.why: Politically unlikely; 'no votes in doing the right thing'.

mechanism_chains.evidence: 1993 versus 2025 comparison, R-G arithmetic, Eichengreen and Dornbusch, term premium logic; the recent pattern that weak data brings yields back down is acknowledged.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: A recession pulls yields down short-term as the Fed eases, but automatic stabilisers widen the deficit, so it delays rather than solves; strong growth or AI productivity could help but lags 10-15 years.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why US exceptionalism implies lower, not higher, future US returns

steps.to: Largely a valuation re-rating (CAPE half of non-US in 1990, double today)
Its required return should be lower
steps.why: Dimson: safer means lower required return, so bullish expected return and required return views are inconsistent.

steps.from: Rich valuations and forward-looking estimates of about 5-6%
steps.to: Below-average equity returns and downside risk, with mean reversion
steps.why: Forward-looking estimates correlate positively with realised returns; drawdowns follow optimism.

mechanism_chains.evidence: AQR papers, Dimson conversation, Global Investment Returns Yearbook (which in 2000 was right on lower returns but wrong on less US outperformance).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Valuation-based forecasts have limits (the 2000 yearbook missed US outperformance); returns can overshoot estimates in both directions.

mechanism_chains.topic: From shifting regime to scenario-based allocation

steps.from: 1980-2020 disinflation and falling yields favoured financial assets and private markets
steps.to: Historical correlations and returns are a poor guide for the new regime

steps.from: Map a portfolio for each macro scenario (stagflation, inflation) and weight by probability
steps.to: Tilt away from financial assets toward real assets, commodities and pure diversifiers
steps.why: More robust than a point estimate; avoids over-weighting the last regime (commodities in 2021).

mechanism_chains.evidence: Investor discussions at London events; no test.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Scenario weights are subjective; Niels points out choosing the wrong scenario can hurt.

mechanism_chains.topic: Hard data patchiness hurts macro-data-based strategies

steps.from: Tariff front-loading, pauses and court rulings
steps.to: Noisy hard data (durable goods -7% after +6-7%) and a gap with pessimistic soft data
steps.why: Single prints mislead; turning point unclear.

steps.to: Trouble for strategies built on high-frequency macro data; falling allocator interest in quant macro
steps.why: Hard to read the economy for months.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Durable goods print; the SG Prime survey.

decision_process.practice: Construct allocations by mapping a portfolio for each macro scenario and weighting by probability, rather than plugging in historical averages or anchoring on 1980-2020.
decision_process.why: The regime is shifting; scenario weights tilt toward real assets, commodities and pure diversifiers.

decision_process.practice: Make the allocation process robust to volatility and correlation assumptions.
decision_process.why: The future may differ from the past.

decision_process.practice: Hold a higher allocation to pure diversifiers (e.g. trend following), diversified across risk factors rather than across labels such as equities, private equity and credit.
decision_process.why: Robustness and shared tail risk among equity-like assets.

decision_process.practice: Form return expectations from forward-looking measures (dividend yield plus earnings growth) rather than trailing returns.
decision_process.why: Forward-looking estimates correlate positively with realised returns; trailing returns correlate negatively.

decision_process.practice: Do not time trend-following allocations on macro or political views; stick with them.
decision_process.why: A macro-linked call may be right for a year before something surprises; consensus arrives late.

decision_process.practice: Read the SG Prime allocator survey, conversations with investors and academic papers (AQR, Dimson, Eichengreen) as inputs to the macro and allocation picture.
decision_process.why: Real-time snapshot of allocator flows and academic evidence on required and expected returns.

speakers.evidence_style: Historical analogy (1993 versus 2025, 1990s deficit reduction, Nixon-Burns), academic papers and conversations with named experts (Eichengreen, Dimson, AQR), arithmetic (R minus G), and conversations with allocators; does not backtest.

current_views.view: US yields are headed higher: 'all roads lead to higher yields', whether this year or next, because of the three-decade trajectory of debt, deficits and policy.
current_views.reasoning: R-G arithmetic, fading bond-market discipline, fiscal dominance, Fed chair risk in 2026.

current_views.view: A recession would pull yields down only temporarily; in the alternative where the economy holds up and near-term inflation rises, a forced Fed response could be the trigger for higher yields.
current_views.reasoning: Pattern of the last two to three years; automatic stabilisers widen the deficit.

current_views.view: Economic data will be hard to read for months; the economy could be turning down but hard data are noisy and soft data are pessimistic.
current_views.reasoning: Tariff front-loading, pause and court rulings.

current_views.view: The JGB yield spike did not trigger yen carry unwinding; the private sector dodged a bullet because the BOJ bought bonds ahead of the move.
Forward-looking measures point to below-average equity returns (about 5-6% for US equities) and downside risk; US equities are expensive after a re-rating.
current_views.reasoning: Required versus expected return inconsistency; rich valuations.

current_views.view: The high-dispersion 2025 environment offers big asymmetric opportunities for discretionary macro, though results vary widely by manager, as April showed.
current_views.reasoning: Dispersion and volatility in macro markets.

current_views.view: Tariff effects on inflation are unclear; reindustrialisation of a full-employment economy may add wage pressure.

Medium-term FX trend positions (long euro, short dollar) turned choppy and range-bound for four to six weeks, and managers were more likely to be long the US short end, which reversed; ultra-slow trend followers did best through the April-May equity V-reversal.

SG Prime spring 2025 survey: global macro, then equity market neutral, then commodities most likely to gain allocations; trend CTA interest about 30%, down 2.5 points from fall 2024; quant macro and ESG interest down; possible performance chasing.
current_views.reasoning: Survey of about 370 allocators, mostly fund of funds, family offices, consultants and wealth.

current_views.reasoning: Observation of multi-strategy performance (speaker attribution uncertain).

current_views.view: Private equity exits packaged for retail may reflect weak institutional demand; low distributions constrain new flows.

worldview_premises.support: Logic only.

worldview_premises.premise: Robust portfolios come from diversification across risk factors, not from strong forecasts in a world changing in ways we cannot imagine.
worldview_premises.support: Assertion.

worldview_premises.premise: When allocators flock to discretionary macro, a non-predictive rules-based diversified approach is useful in unpredictable policy regimes; otherwise outcomes are a coin flip.

disagreements.topic: Scenario-based allocation versus a regime-agnostic trend allocation

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Map portfolios for macro scenarios and weight by probability; tilt to real assets, commodities and pure diversifiers.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Choosing among scenarios raises the risk of choosing wrongly; regime-agnostic trend following covers risks nobody planned for.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: How on earth can one make sense of this world discretionarily; it is almost a coin flip, so a rules-based diversified approach is more useful.

disagreements.topic: Can AI-driven growth ease the debt problem

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: An AI boom is part of the narrative and might even let the Fed cut deeply (his 2024 'outrageous prediction' of 1%); stronger growth would solve things.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Productivity gains typically lag new technology by 10-15 years and labour force growth is limited, so growth will not fix the debt soon.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The thesis is directional but without timing ('this year or next'); Alan notes recession would pull yields down short-term, which conflicts with 'all roads lead to higher yields' unless the horizon is stated.

R greater than G is described as making debt unsustainable regardless of the debt/GDP level, yet the current 10-year yield is said to be roughly equal to nominal growth (4-4.5%); the threshold for 'the break' (5%) is asserted, not derived.
Real yields about 2% versus over 3% in 1993 are used both to show rising term premia and that they may decouple from inflation; no term-premium estimate is given.
Speaker corrections: the macro-view-timing points (C17-3, C17-6) are Alan's; pod-shop remark (C13-2) may be shared between speakers.
Valuation-based forecasting is endorsed as the better guide even though the same source (Yearbook) was wrong on US outperformance; Alan accepts this limit but does not say how much weight to give it.
The dismissal of the carry-trade unwind (dollar-yen stayed in range) is explained by several possibilities (insurers shifting, BOJ buying) without evidence for any.
Unverified headline claims relayed by the host (Bitcoin market cap above Alphabet; Thoma Bravo remark; Stargate energy use).

Niels says allocators flocking to macro suggests performance chasing; Alan says the survey results are unsurprising; neither shows evidence of chasing, and the survey percentages are quoted from memory.
The Port of Los Angeles remark is evidence for shipping lead times but is not tied to any trade or forecast.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs that Alan says lead yields: the 10-year yield relative to nominal GDP growth (4-4.5%; a move to 5% or above breaks R-G), the deficit and debt path (2025 budget bill, Treasury reliance on bills), term premium and the stock-bond correlation (hedge value), Fed leadership after Powell's term ends in 2026, and near-term inflation forcing a Fed response. Horizon is 'this year or next' for the direction and decades for fiscal dominance. For equities he uses forward-looking return estimates (dividend yield plus earnings growth) with a 10-year horizon. Niels offers no predictive input: trend signals, the Trend Barometer and model speed describe the state of trend performance, and he says trend allocations should not be tied to macro views.
reader_inferences: (reader) Alan's chain implies a testable relationship: episodes when the 10-year yield exceeded nominal GDP growth with rising debt/GDP should show higher subsequent term premia; he gives no sample.
(reader) The disagreement over scenarios versus trend suggests a combined approach: scenario-based core with trend as the untimed residual for unplanned risks.

(reader) Both speakers treat the weak-data environment as bad for macro-data-driven strategies, which would predict relatively better results for price-based trend, but May 2025 results were poor for trend as well.

(reader) The pattern Alan describes (deficit worries fade on weak data and return) implies yields at a given growth state should be higher than in earlier cycles, an effect observable in the level of yields at similar unemployment rates.
